meta.title: Who really said "All I need is a sheet of paper and something to write with, and then I can turn the world upside down"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Nietzsche never wrote this. It first appears as a made-up epigraph in Cornelia Funke's novel Inkspell (2005), credited there to a fictional Nietzsche book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'All I need is a sheet of paper and something to write with, and then I can turn the world upside down'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Nietzsche. The line originates as a fabricated epigraph in Cornelia Funke's Inkspell (2005), attributed to a Nietzsche work that doesn't exist.

answer.label: Not Nietzsche — from Cornelia Funke's Inkheart trilogy
answer.authorDates: born 1958 · German children’s & YA fantasy author
answer.sourceLine: This is not Nietzsche at all. The earliest documented appearance of the line is the epigraph to chapter 26 of Cornelia Funke’s novel Inkspell (2005), where Funke playfully credits it to a Nietzsche book that does not exist — Die Weiße und die Schwarze Kunst. As the MLA Style Center documents, Nietzsche never wrote a work by that title, and the wording turns up in none of his actual books.

source.excerpt: All I need is a sheet of paper and something to write with, and then I can turn the world upside down.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under Misattributed, calling it “most likely from Cornelia Funke’s Inkheart trilogy.”
The MLA Style Center pins it to the epigraph of chapter 26 of Inkspell, attributed there to a Nietzsche title that “appears to be fictional.”
Inkspell (German Tintenblut) is a 2005 novel by Cornelia Funke, translated by Anthea Bell — a modern, in-copyright work.
Quote aggregators such as Goodreads still file the line under Nietzsche with no source, which is how the misattribution kept spreading.
source.excerptNote: In the novel this stands as a chapter epigraph, printed under Nietzsche’s name and an invented book title — a literary flourish that later escaped the page and spread online as a real Nietzsche quotation.

author.metaLine: born 1958 · German author of the Inkheart (Tintenwelt) fantasy trilogy
author.bio: Cornelia Funke (born 1958) is a German author of children’s and young-adult fantasy, best known for the Inkheart (Tintenwelt) trilogy — Inkheart, Inkspell, and Inkdeath — whose central conceit is that words read aloud can literally reshape the world. Fittingly, the disputed line first surfaces inside that trilogy as a chapter epigraph she credits to an invented Nietzsche title, a flourish that later escaped the book and circulated online as a genuine Nietzsche quotation.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet-name” misattribution: an appealing line about the power of the pen, pinned on a famous philosopher who never wrote it.

items.why: Wikiquote files the line under Misattributed, and the MLA Style Center found it in none of Nietzsche’s works, which are widely searchable online.

items.who: “Die Weiße und die Schwarze Kunst” (a fictional Nietzsche book)
items.why: In Inkspell, Funke credits the epigraph to this title, but as the MLA Style Center notes, “Nietzsche never wrote a book by this title, which appears to be fictional.”

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented source is Cornelia Funke’s own novel Inkspell (2005), where the line is a made-up epigraph — not anything Nietzsche said or wrote.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Nietzsche
lead: The idea — that a writer armed with only paper and pen can overturn the world — sits perfectly inside Funke’s Inkworld, where words read aloud literally remake reality. So a boastful line about the power of writing felt at home as an epigraph, and Nietzsche’s reputation for punchy aphorisms made the fictional credit read as plausible.

Once the line was lifted out of the novel and onto quote sites, the fabricated citation fell away and only the famous name remained — a self-reinforcing loop, since no aggregator ever names the Nietzsche work it supposedly comes from (because none exists).
context.pull: A line invented for a novel about the magic of writing became — through writing — a fake Nietzsche quote.
